item.title: Deputies Dataset 2002-2026
item.description: This dataset provides ideological position estimates for members of the Chilean Chamber of Deputies across six consecutive legislative periods, spanning from 2002 to 2026 in four-year intervals. The estimates are based exclusively on roll-call votes related to bill proposals debated and voted on in the plenary sessions. It excludes other types of votes, such as those on non-binding agreements or investigative commissions, which do not directly contribute to lawmaking. item.title: Network Disadoption: exposure to disadoption as an indicator of social contagion
item.description: Research on the diffusion of innovations has focused on adoption: moving from not using to using a practice. Its natural counterpart, disadoption (stopping its use), has received far less attention, even though it is a substantively different process. This project asks whether abandoning a behavior also spreads through the network, and how to measure that influence. The work is carried out by Aníbal Olivera in collaboration with Thomas W. Valente and the team at the Center for Applied Network Analysis (USC).

item.title: Networks Decide for Us: network structure as a causal force in diffusion
item.description: The diffusion of collective behaviors is usually modeled as the outcome of individual decisions or as a contagion process. This project starts from a different question: if we hold each person’s propensities fixed, does diffusion change just because the shape of the network changes? The argument is that networks “decide for us”: relational structure, shaped by homophily, enables or constrains social change beyond the sum of individual preferences. The project is carried out by Aníbal Olivera and Jorge Fábrega (CICS, UDD) together with Thomas W.

item.title: Political Networks: collaboration in the Constitutional Convention (2021–2022)
item.description: Chile’s Constitutional Convention (2021–2022) is a rare natural experiment for studying how political collaboration organizes from scratch: a majority of delegates with no prior political experience, a body that dissolved upon delivering its draft, and procedural rules written by its own members. Two of those rules structure the study. Each constitutional initiative required between 8 and 16 signatures, so signing amounted to forming a visible, dated coalition. In addition, each provision needed two thirds of the plenary (103 of 154 votes) to pass.
